gloss_terse: Ahijah / Ahiyahu -- proper name meaning 'brother of Yah(weh),' borne by a prophet, priest, scribe, and others
gloss_readable: A theophoric name compounded from 'ach ('brother') and Yah ('the LORD'), meaning 'my brother is Yahweh.' It appears in two spelling variants: the shorter Ahijah (אֲחִיָּה) and the longer Ahiyahu (אֲחִיָּהוּ). The most prominent bearer is Ahijah the Shilonite, the prophet who tore his new garment into twelve pieces to symbolize the coming division of Solomon's kingdom (1 Kgs 11:29-30) and who later pronounced doom on Jeroboam's dynasty (1 Kgs 14:1-18). Other bearers include a priest under Saul (1 Sam 14:3), a royal scribe (1 Kgs 4:3), and the father of King Baasha (1 Kgs 15:27).

senses.1: A proper masculine name meaning 'brother of Yah(weh),' applied to at least six distinct individuals in the Hebrew Bible. The most theologically significant is Ahijah the Shilonite prophet who foretold the northern secession by tearing his garment into twelve pieces (1 Kgs 11:29-30) and later pronounced judgment on Jeroboam's house (1 Kgs 14:1-18). English, Spanish, French, and German translations consistently transliterate the name with minor orthographic variation (Achiyah, Ahías, Ahija). The Phoenician parallel 'achimelech' confirms the kinship-theophoric naming pattern.

gloss_terse: Calamity, disaster, sudden ruin -- devastating misfortune as divine judgment or consequence of wickedness
gloss_readable: A poetic and prophetic term for sudden, overwhelming disaster. Found almost exclusively in Wisdom literature and the later prophets, this word conveys catastrophe crashing down upon its victims -- whether apostate Israel, foreign nations, or the wicked individual. In Proverbs 1:26-27 personified Wisdom laughs when calamity overtakes those who spurned her counsel. The Arabic cognate suggests something that 'burdens' or 'bends' a person under its weight. Deuteronomy 32:35 anchors it in the theology of divine retribution: 'the day of their calamity is near.' Translations across languages converge on terms for sudden devastation: Spanish calamidad, French calamité.

senses.1: Sudden, devastating calamity or ruin, used in poetic and prophetic contexts for catastrophic misfortune. Applied nationally to Israel's apostasy (Jer 18:17), to foreign nations under divine judgment such as Moab (Jer 48:16) and Edom (Jer 49:8; Obad 13), and personally to the righteous sufferer (2 Sam 22:19; Ps 18:19) and the wicked reaping consequences (Job 18:12; 21:17; Prov 1:26-27). The Arabic cognate meaning 'burdening' captures the crushing weight this word implies. Deuteronomy 32:35 anchors it squarely in the theology of divine retribution, while Proverbs presents it as the natural harvest of folly.

gloss_terse: Locust -- the swarming migratory grasshopper, devastating crop-destroyer and figure for invading armies
gloss_readable: The common swarming locust, a migratory grasshopper species that appears in immense clouds capable of stripping entire landscapes bare. Closely associated with the Egyptian plagues (Exod 10:4-19), where God sends and then removes the swarm by a mighty east wind, this word denotes both literal agricultural devastation and serves as a vivid simile for innumerable invading armies (Judg 6:5; 7:12). Joel 1:4 places it in a four-species sequence depicting total crop destruction. Leviticus 11:22 lists it among clean insects permitted for food. German Heuschrecke, Spanish langosta, and French sauterelle all converge on the same well-known insect.

senses.1: The swarming locust, a migratory grasshopper appearing in devastating multitudes. Primarily associated with the Egyptian plague narrative (Exod 10:4-19), where it functions as an instrument of divine judgment. Listed among clean insects permitted for food (Lev 11:22). Frequently deployed in simile for overwhelming multitudes -- the Midianite hordes are 'like locusts for number' (Judg 6:5; 7:12). Joel 1:4 places it in a sequence with three other locust species to depict total agricultural devastation. Multilingual evidence is uniform: Spanish langosta, German Heuschrecke, French sauterelle all point to the same well-recognized insect.

gloss_terse: Boaz -- kinsman-redeemer of Ruth in Bethlehem; also the name of the left pillar in Solomon's temple
gloss_readable: Best known as the generous landowner of Bethlehem who became Ruth's kinsman-redeemer, marrying the Moabite widow and thus entering the ancestral line of David and ultimately of Jesus the Messiah (Ruth 2-4; Matt 1:5). The etymology is debated -- possibly 'in him is strength' or 'swiftness.' The name also designates the left-hand bronze pillar erected before Solomon's temple (1 Kgs 7:21; 2 Chr 3:17), perhaps inscribed as a memorial or bearing the meaning 'in strength.' The Septuagint of 2 Chronicles 3:17 renders it as ischus ('strength'), preserving this etymological thread. A minor Calebite descendant also bears the name (1 Chr 2:11-12).

senses.1: The proper name Boaz (בֹּעַז), referring primarily to the wealthy Bethlehemite kinsman-redeemer who married Ruth the Moabitess (Ruth 2-4), securing the Davidic and messianic lineage. Also designates the left pillar at Solomon's temple entrance (1 Kgs 7:21; 2 Chr 3:17), where the LXX of Chronicles renders it as ischus ('strength'), hinting at the possible etymology 'in him is strength.' The German rendering in-Kraft for the pillar occurrence uniquely preserves this etymological interpretation across translation traditions. A minor Calebite figure also bears the name (1 Chr 2:47).

gloss_terse: Bear good tidings, announce joyful news -- proclaim victory, salvation, or glad tidings (Piel stem)
gloss_readable: In the Piel stem, this verb means to bring or proclaim good news, with a rich semantic range spanning battlefield victory reports, prophetic announcements of salvation, and liturgical praise. The Arabic cognate connects the joy of the face with delivering glad tidings. Isaiah's herald crying 'Your God reigns!' (Isa 52:7) represents the theological summit of this word, later echoed in the New Testament concept of 'gospel' (euangelion). The feminine participle mevasseret (Isa 40:9) personifies Zion herself as the bearer of good news. Psalm 96:2 extends the word into communal worship: 'proclaim his salvation day after day.' Spanish anunciad and French annoncer capture its proclamatory force.

senses.1: To bear or proclaim good tidings, especially news of military victory or divine deliverance (Piel). The battlefield messenger who runs to announce the outcome of war is the paradigmatic usage (2 Sam 18:19-20; 1 Sam 31:9). Isaiah transforms this into eschatological proclamation -- the herald announces God's reign and salvation to Zion (Isa 40:9; 41:27; 52:7; 61:1). The participial form mevasser becomes a technical term for prophetic announcement, and Psalm 96:2 extends it to liturgical worship. The Arabic cognate bashar links the joy of the face with delivering glad news, while the Ethiopic cognate absara confirms the joyful-announcement sense across Semitic languages.

gloss_terse: Expire, breathe one's last, perish -- die, especially of patriarchs; emphasizes the moment life departs
gloss_readable: A solemn verb for the act of dying, emphasizing the final exhalation -- the moment breath leaves the body. Found exclusively in the Priestly source and in poetry, it carries a quiet dignity distinct from the common verb muth ('to die'). The patriarchal death notices use it formulaically: Abraham 'expired and died at a good old age' (Gen 25:8), as did Ishmael (Gen 25:17) and Isaac (Gen 35:29). In Job and the Psalms it expresses both the fragility of mortal life -- when God withdraws breath, creatures expire and return to dust (Job 34:15; Ps 104:29) -- and the anguish of approaching death (Ps 88:16). The flood narrative employs it for the universal perishing of all flesh (Gen 6:17; 7:21).

senses.1: To expire, breathe one's last, perish -- marking the precise moment life departs. Restricted to the Priestly source and poetic texts, this verb dignifies the death of the patriarchs: Abraham (Gen 25:8), Ishmael (Gen 25:17), Isaac (Gen 35:29), and Jacob (Gen 49:33) all 'expire' in formulaic death notices. In the flood account it describes universal perishing (Gen 6:17; 7:21). In Wisdom poetry it conveys mortal fragility -- when God withdraws his breath, creatures expire and return to dust (Job 34:15; Ps 104:29). Often paired with muth ('die') or 'avad ('perish') for intensification (Num 17:27-28; Job 3:11).

gloss_terse: Sickness, disease, illness -- physical malady or affliction, sometimes metaphorical for national distress
gloss_readable: Denotes physical sickness or disease in its various manifestations, from the fatal illness of a widow's son (1 Kgs 17:17) to the chronic foot disease of King Asa (2 Chr 16:12) to the collective plagues threatened in the Deuteronomic covenant curses (Deut 7:15; 28:59, 61). The word reaches its theological depth in Isaiah 53:3-4, where the Suffering Servant is described as one 'acquainted with sickness' who has borne 'our diseases.' Hosea 5:13 extends it metaphorically to the spiritual sickness of a wayward nation that seeks healing from Assyria rather than from God. Multilingual glosses converge cleanly: Spanish enfermedad, German Krankheit, pointing to a concrete, recognizable concept across cultures.

senses.1: Physical sickness, disease, or illness affecting individuals or communities. Appears in covenantal contexts for plagues God will inflict or withhold (Deut 7:15; 28:59, 61), and in narrative for specific afflictions: the fatal illness of the widow's son at Zarephath (1 Kgs 17:17), Ahaziah's injury (2 Kgs 1:2), Elisha's terminal sickness (2 Kgs 13:14), and Asa's diseased feet (2 Chr 16:12). Reaches its theological summit in Isaiah 53:3-4, where the Servant vicariously bears human suffering, parallel to makh'ov ('pain'). Metaphorically applied to national distress in Hosea 5:13 and Isaiah 1:5, signaling spiritual decay that no human alliance can heal.

gloss_terse: Jabesh -- city of Jabesh-Gilead in Transjordan; also the father of King Shallum of Israel
gloss_readable: Primarily designates the Transjordanian city of Jabesh-Gilead, a settlement east of the Jordan in the territory of Gilead. The city figures prominently in Israel's early history: its inhabitants were punished for refusing to join the assembly against Benjamin (Judg 21:8-14), Saul's first royal act was to rescue it from Nahash the Ammonite's brutal siege (1 Sam 11:1-11), and its grateful citizens later recovered Saul's body from the walls of Beth-shan after his death on Gilboa (1 Sam 31:11-13; 2 Sam 2:4-5). This reciprocal loyalty between Saul and Jabesh is one of the most poignant threads in the Samuel narrative. As a personal name, Jabesh is the father of Shallum, a usurper king of the northern kingdom (2 Kgs 15:10-14).

senses.1: The proper name Jabesh (יָבֵשׁ / יָבֵישׁ), used primarily as a place-name for Jabesh-Gilead in Transjordan and secondarily as a patronymic. The city is central to three pivotal narratives: the Benjaminite wife-procurement after the civil war (Judg 21:8-14), Saul's heroic deliverance from Ammonite siege (1 Sam 11:1-11), and the loyal recovery of Saul's remains by its grateful citizens (1 Sam 31:11-13; 2 Sam 2:4-5). As a personal name, Jabesh is the father of Shallum who assassinated Zechariah (2 Kgs 15:10, 13-14). Translations uniformly transliterate: Jabesh, Jabès (French), Jabes (Spanish).

gloss_terse: Jotham -- proper name meaning 'YHWH is perfect,' borne by Gideon's youngest son and a king of Judah
gloss_readable: A theophoric name meaning 'Yahweh is perfect' or 'YHWH is complete,' borne by three biblical figures. The most dramatic is Jotham son of Gideon (Jerubbaal), sole survivor of Abimelech's massacre of seventy brothers, who delivered the famous fable of the trees seeking a king from atop Mount Gerizim (Judg 9:5-21). The most politically significant is Jotham king of Judah, son of Uzziah, who governed as regent during his father's leprosy and reigned in his own right (2 Kgs 15:5-38; 2 Chr 27). His name anchors the superscriptions of Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah, placing their prophecies chronologically. A minor Calebite figure also bears the name (1 Chr 2:47).

senses.1: The proper masculine name Yotam (יוֹתָם), meaning 'YHWH is perfect/complete,' designating three individuals. Most memorably, Jotham son of Gideon escaped Abimelech's fratricide and pronounced his parable of the bramble-king from Mount Gerizim (Judg 9:5-21, 57). Jotham king of Judah served first as regent during his leprous father Uzziah's quarantine, then as sole ruler (2 Kgs 15:5, 32-38; 2 Chr 26:21-27:9), and appears in the prophetic dating formulae of Isaiah 1:1, Hosea 1:1, and Micah 1:1. A minor Calebite figure also bears the name (1 Chr 2:47). Translations transliterate consistently: Jotham, Jotam (Spanish/German), Yotam.

gloss_terse: Capital of a pillar -- the ornamental crown atop a column, especially the temple pillars Jachin and Boaz
gloss_readable: A specialized architectural term for the capital -- the ornamental top piece crowning a pillar or column. All 24 occurrences cluster tightly around the description of Solomon's temple furnishings, particularly the elaborate bronze capitals atop the two freestanding pillars named Jachin and Boaz (1 Kgs 7:16-42). These capitals were decorated with lattice-work, rows of pomegranates, and lily-shaped designs, standing five cubits high and representing some of the finest craftsmanship in ancient Israel. The root suggests 'surrounding' or 'crowning,' aptly describing how a capital encircles and adorns the top of its column. The parallel accounts in 2 Kings 25:17 and Jeremiah 52:22 recall these same capitals in the solemn context of Babylon's destruction of the temple.

senses.1: The ornamental capital or crown atop a pillar, used exclusively in architectural descriptions of Solomon's temple and its destruction. All occurrences refer to the elaborately decorated bronze capitals on the pillars Jachin and Boaz (1 Kgs 7:16-42), with parallel descriptions in the destruction narrative (2 Kgs 25:17; Jer 52:22). These five-cubit-high capitals featured intricate lattice-work, rows of pomegranates, and lily-shaped designs. The root suggests 'encircling' or 'crowning,' capturing how the capital surrounds and adorns the column's summit. Spanish capitel and equivalent terms across languages all point to this specific architectural element.
